questions.question: What does .* do in a regular expression?
explanations: Correct. . matches any character and * means 0 or more times; together they match any sequence.
No. For exactly one character it would be just the dot (.).
No. For digits or letters it would be \w.
No. For spaces it would be \s.

questions.question: What is greedy vs lazy in regular expressions?
options: Greedy takes the maximum, lazy takes the minimum
Greedy is fast, lazy is slow
Greedy matches everything, lazy matches nothing
explanations: Correct. Greedy tries to match the largest amount possible; lazy tries to match the smallest amount possible.
No. Speed is not the difference; it is the amount of text they try to match.
No. Lazy does not match nothing; it matches the smallest amount possible.
No. There is a difference; greedy uses * and lazy uses *?.

questions.question: How do you check if an email is valid using regex?
explanations: Correct. A Pattern is created with a regular expression that defines the email format and is validated with Matcher.
No. There is no isEmail() method in Java.
No. contains(@) only checks that it has @; it does not validate the full format.
No. It can be validated using regular expressions.

questions.question: What is a capture group in regular expressions?
options: Parentheses that group part of the pattern
Angle brackets that mark start and end
explanations: Correct. Parentheses () create capture groups that allow extracting specific parts of the matched text.
No. Braces {} are used for quantifiers, not for capture.
No. Brackets [] define character classes.
No. Angle brackets <> are not used in regex.

questions.question: What does \b do in a regular expression?
explanations: Correct. \b represents a boundary between a word and a whitespace, useful for searching whole words.
No. For spaces you use \s, not \b.
No. For line breaks you use \n, not \b.
No. It is not a backspace; it is a word boundary.
